Moonshot AI has released the Kimi K3.1 Pro model weights, an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model that builds on the Kimi K3 series with enhanced long-context modeling and a 1-million-token context window. Kimi K3.1 Pro replaces previous full-attention layers with more efficient Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers and has been evaluated on multiple coding and agentic benchmarks using Claude Code and other evaluation harnesses. The model demonstrates substantial improvements over prior versions and other contemporary models in various specialized tasks.

items.title: Anthropic advances zkSNARK cryptographic proofs for AI model inference, enabling verification that responses come from claimed models with improved efficiency [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Progress on provable inference for large language models
items.summary:
Anthropic has developed a system called FlashProve that uses zkSNARK cryptographic proofs to verify that AI model responses are generated by the claimed model, addressing concerns about model substitution or tampering. This system achieves significantly faster proof generation speeds on large models like Llama 4 Maverick, using a single H100 GPU to produce proofs at around 110 tokens per second with manageable proof sizes.

The research includes releasing technical documentation, executable code, and formal verification proofs under an open-source license to encourage further development. This work aims to enhance trust and security in AI model deployment, particularly for applications requiring assurance of model integrity and compliance verification.

items.title: Researchers introduce Agent Harness Awareness to provide verified telemetry snapshots for tool-using AI agents, reducing policy regret by 96.9% and improving task completion rates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents
items.summary: Agent Harness Awareness is a new design that addresses operational blindness in AI agents by supplying verified, up-to-date state snapshots before executing significant actions. This approach allows models to make better-informed decisions by integrating host telemetry data while the host retains control over enforcement and dispatch authority. Experiments with models including GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash showed a 96.9% reduction in policy regret and an increase in single-dispatch task completion from 69.4% to 95.8%. Additional tests with live local execution and fault injection confirmed the method's effectiveness in reducing operational costs and improving reliability. The study suggests further exploration of runtime state, hardware pressure, and recovery mechanisms within this architecture.

items.title: Researchers propose challenge-aware adaptive recruitment with meta-agent supervision to improve multi-agent reasoning in medical question answering, boosting accuracy on biomedical benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment with Meta-Agent Supervision for Medical Multi-Agent Reasoning
items.summary:
A new study introduces challenge-aware adaptive recruitment, a method that uses an external component called the CHALLENGER to monitor reasoning processes and identify knowledge gaps during medical multi-agent reasoning tasks. This approach enables targeted retrieval of information and specialist agent recruitment, improving performance over traditional upfront retrieval methods.

Experiments on the MEDAGENTSBENCH benchmark, covering nine biomedical datasets, show that this method enhances accuracy on eight of nine datasets and raises GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%. The study highlights the importance of timing and coordination in integrating external resources for complex medical reasoning, as naive combinations of retrieval and specialist recruitment can degrade performance.

items.title: SlackBench benchmarks AI agents on collaborative research projects using real code repositories and multi-party communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SlackBench: Benchmarking Agents on Collaborative Projects Grounded in Real Code Repositories
items.summary:
SlackBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on realistic research and engineering workflows that involve reasoning over workplace communication and evolving code repositories. It uses privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic projects, combining multi-party dialogues, decision-making, and code changes from GitHub and Google Docs to simulate complex collaborative environments.

The benchmark includes 140 queries covering tasks such as multi-source search, abstention on unanswerable questions, goal-directed summarization, and inference over long conversations. Testing across 33 advanced models showed the best system scoring around 80%, with most below 66%, indicating significant room for improvement. SlackBench offers an extensible framework for assessing AI agents in collaborative work settings, and its dataset is publicly available.
items.description:
SlackBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on realistic research and engineering workflows that involve reasoning over workplace communication and evolving code repositories. It uses privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic projects, combining multi-party dialogues, decision-making, and code changes from GitHub and Google Docs to simulate complex collaborative environments.

The benchmark includes 140 queries covering tasks such as multi-source search, abstention on unanswerable questions, goal-directed summarization, and inference over long conversations. Testing across 33 advanced models showed the best system scoring around 80%, with most below 66%, indicating significant room for improvement. SlackBench offers an extensible framework for assessing AI agents in collaborative work settings, and its dataset is publicly available.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI Agents are becoming digital coworkers that can browse the web, write code, run experiments, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of real knowledge work: many rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks, missing the complex, multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code, and evolving decisions. Even simple workplace questions may require locating relevant channels and direct messages, recovering context from long discussions, inspecting repository state, reconciling stale or conflicting evidence, and synthesizing across sources. We introduce SlackBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on realistic research and engineering workflows that require joint reasoning over workplace communication and evolving repository state. Grounded in privacy-preserving reenactments of real academic research projects, SlackBench provides reproducible environments with realistic multi-party dialogue, evolving decisions, and corresponding code changes grounded in GitHub repositories and Google Docs. It contains 140 queries spanning heterogeneous-source agentic search, abstention on unanswerable or false-premise questions, goal-directed summarization, and circumstance inference over long conversations. These tasks are not reducible to static corpus question answering: agents must determine which conversations matter, traverse threads, inspect repository state, and synthesize evidence across communication and code artifacts. Across 33 frontier models and agent harnesses, the best system scores around 80% and most agents score below 66%, highlighting substantial headroom for improvement. SlackBench thus provides an extensible framework for evaluating agents in collaborative work environments. The SlackBench dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuanzhiMao/SlackBench .

items.title: Researchers evaluate seven AI language models creating, grading, and revising data science projects over three rounds, finding average scores improve from 59% to 76% with feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
items.summary: Researchers tested seven AI language models from five developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, to assess their ability to complete end-to-end data science projects involving data handling and report writing. Each model acted as both a writer and grader in 49 pairings, with projects iterated through three rounds of creation, grading, and revision. The study found that average project scores increased from 59% initially to 76% after the final round, with improvements varying by model and role. Models grading their own work tended to assign higher scores than others, and feedback generally led to the highest score gains, though some models improved with revision opportunities alone. The effectiveness of the iterative loop depended on the combination of models in writer and grader roles, with weaker models rarely improving stronger ones.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Z.AI. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.

items.title: AGORA proposes item-response-theory-based aggregation of LLM judges to improve reliability weighting without human labels, outperforming Dawid-Skene on small evaluation sets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AGORA: Reliability-Aware Aggregation of LLM Judges via Item-Response Theory
items.summary:
AGORA introduces a method to aggregate large language model (LLM) judges by modeling each item's latent quality and each judge's sensitivity and rating thresholds, enabling reliability assessment without human-labeled data. This approach addresses the challenge of judge pools with varying reliability and limited human-labeled validation sets, where traditional methods like Dawid-Skene struggle to estimate per-judge error accurately.
Across three benchmarks, AGORA matches or exceeds the performance of Dawid-Skene on large evaluation sets and shows greater advantages as the number of items decreases to a few hundred. It maintains accuracy with uneven judge pools, uses a label-free dispersion statistic to predict when trust weighting is beneficial, and its learned trust weights correlate with human validity assessments per judge.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge is a common substitute for costly human evaluation, and aggregating several judges is the standard remedy for any single judge's bias. Judge pools mix judges of very different reliability, while the human-labeled sets that validate them hold a few hundred items or fewer. In this regime the per-item mean weights weak judges as heavily as strong ones, and confusion-table models such as Dawid-Skene must estimate a per-judge error table from too few items. We propose AGORA (Aggregation Of Reliability-weighted Assessments), an item-response-theory aggregator that places every item on one latent quality scale and describes each judge by a sensitivity parameter and ordered rating thresholds, so judge reliability is learned from all items jointly and without human labels. Across three benchmarks, AGORA matches or exceeds Dawid-Skene on large evaluation sets, and its advantage widens as the set shrinks toward a few hundred items. It remains accurate as pools grow more uneven, a label-free dispersion statistic indicates in advance when trust weighting helps, and its learned trust weights track per-judge human validity.

items.title: Researchers find confirmation bias affects Agent-as-a-Judge evaluators despite evidence grounding, overturning up to 40% of correct verdicts across multiple judges and datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Grounded but Not Immune: Confirmation Bias in Agent-as-a-judge
items.summary:
Researchers studied Agent-as-a-Judge systems that evaluate open-ended agent tasks by verifying results against the environment using tools and full agent trajectories. They found that these judges are susceptible to confirmation bias: a single false pre-screening note attributed to an authority, but irrelevant to the correct verdict, caused up to 40% of correct decisions to be overturned across four judges and five datasets, despite the judges collecting decisive evidence.

The study identifies three failure modes driving this bias: over-trust (accepting and deferring to the false cue after correct verification), hallucination (fabricating support for the incorrect flip), and under-investigation (stopping early after the first corroborating signal). For larger Claude judges, over-trust accounted for most harmful flips, while smaller judges exhibited all three error modes. The researchers treated the false cue as a diagnostic tool rather than an adversarial attack and found that lightweight mitigations reduce but do not eliminate the bias.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating open-ended agent tasks increasingly falls to an Agent-as-a-Judge: an evaluator handed tools and the agent's full trajectory so it can verify a result against the environment. The premise is that a judge that gathers its own evidence should be grounded by it. We show that this grounding does not immunize the judge against confirmation bias: a single false pre-screening note, attributed to an authority and carrying no evidential bearing on the correct verdict, overturns up to 40% of a tool-using judge's correct verdicts across four judges and five datasets, even though the judge collects decisive evidence. The shift is driven by specific properties of the cue. We treat this cue as a controlled diagnostic of confirmation bias rather than an adversarial attack. Our central contribution is to explain how confirmation bias changes the judge's behavior in a trajectory. We classify changes in judge behavior and attribute changes to one of three failure modes: over-trust (verify, conclude correctly, then defer), hallucination (fabricate support for the flip), and under-investigation (stop at the first corroborating signal). For the two Claude judges, the failure is predominantly over-trust (67-75% of harmful flips), while smaller judges have error modes spread across all three. Lightweight mitigations blunt but never remove the bias.

items.title: Researchers test whether large language models can predict AI agents' success on 1,494 real freelance jobs using the PAYWORTHY dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PAYWORTHY: Can LLMs Predict Which Freelance Jobs an AI Agent Will Complete?
items.summary:
Researchers introduced PAYWORTHY, a dataset of 1,494 freelance job postings sampled from 18.8 million listings between 2020 and 2026, to evaluate if large language models (LLMs) can forecast an AI agent's likelihood of completing freelance jobs successfully. They had an AI agent attempt each job once, with an LLM judge deciding whether to accept the work, and tested 18 models on their ability to rank accepted jobs above rejected ones using AUC metrics.
The study found that model predictions depended on how the AI agent was described: when models were informed about the agent's limitations, they ranked jobs well (AUC 0.66–0.86), but when told the agent was a generic one with browsing and code execution capabilities, rankings were near random (AUC 0.45–0.56). These results were consistent across judges from multiple model families and aligned with human raters' verdicts. The researchers have made their code publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before an AI agent takes on a paid job, someone has to judge whether it is likely to succeed. We test whether frontier language models can make this call before any attempt. We propose PAYWORTHY which contains 1{,}494 real freelance job postings, sampled from 18.8M postings made between 2020 and 2026 on a freelancing platform. An agent attempts each job from the posting alone in a single run, and an LLM judge acting as the client decides whether to accept the work. We ask 18 models to forecast how likely the agent is to succeed and measure how well each model's forecasts rank the accepted jobs above the rejected ones (AUC, where 0.5 is a random ranking). The answer depends on how the agent is described. Told what the agent cannot do, every model ranks the jobs well (AUC 0.66--0.86). Told instead that it is a generic agent with a browser and code execution, the same models rank the same jobs about as well as a random ordering (0.45--0.56). These results hold under judges from four other model families (Claude, GLM, Kimi and Qwen), and the informed forecasts also rank the verdicts of two human raters. Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Payworthy

items.title: Researchers present autonomous agents for electricity system planning under carbon constraints across multiple countries and scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Autonomous agents for electricity-system planning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an autonomous planning framework that uses agents to propose and revise electricity system designs, incorporating investment, operation, and network constraints while adhering to carbon budgets. The framework automates annual investment and dispatch optimization, evaluates multiple scenarios across five electricity systems in four countries, and retains the lowest-cost plans meeting emissions and operational criteria.

The study evaluated forty carbon-constrained trajectories using single- and multi-agent architectures, with most designs meeting or exceeding emissions ceilings. An additional archive of ninety-six trajectories under a common 1,000 Mt annual carbon ceiling provides broader regional coverage. The results demonstrate the feasibility of autonomous electricity system planning using public regional data and institutional demand forecasts under explicit emissions constraints.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planning electricity systems requires repeated decisions that connect regional resources, investment, operation and network constraints. Here we present an autonomous planning framework that carries prepared regional scenarios through proposal, numerical evaluation, feedback interpretation, redesign and final plan selection. Agents propose investment bounds, storage operating conditions and feeder interventions, interpret numerical feedback, and decide how to revise designs and when to stop. The framework automatically executes annual investment-and-dispatch optimization and representative-feeder verification, applies fixed acceptance criteria and retains the lowest-cost accepted candidate. We evaluate forty carbon-constrained trajectories across ten system-year scenarios in five electricity systems and four countries, using two model deployments and single- and multi-agent architectures. All forty retain candidates satisfying the implemented physical and fixed annual operational carbon-budget checks. Twenty-eight of forty matched reference designs exceed the new scenario ceilings. A separate archive of ninety-six trajectories under a common 1,000 Mt annual ceiling provides matched references and broader regional coverage. The results demonstrate autonomous planning under explicit emissions constraints using public regional data and published institutional demand outlooks.

items.title: Researchers use Mixture-of-Experts routers to identify and control reasoning behaviors in AI models, reducing overthinking and test-time compute by up to 63% across multiple domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Routes of Reasoning: Reading and Reshaping Test-Time Compute in MoE Models
items.summary:
Researchers demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers can classify distinct reasoning behaviors such as planning, execution, and reflection in AI models without additional training. By labeling sentence-level segments with these behaviors and probing router logits, they achieve behavior prediction comparable to full hidden state analysis but with fewer features. This approach generalizes across six datasets spanning math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense domains.

Building on this insight, the team selectively edits expert router scores during inference to reduce overthinking, cutting generated tokens by a median of 30.4% and up to 63.3% without significant accuracy loss. This method encourages models to stop reasoning once a problem is solved rather than skipping essential steps, offering an interpretable and efficient mechanism to optimize test-time compute in MoE models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning models allocate test-time compute across distinct behaviors such as planning, deriving, and verifying. However, models frequently "overthink," continuing to verify and re-derive long after finding a correct answer. This wastes expensive compute and can even degrade performance. Existing interventions, such as token budgets or steering, primarily regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors. In this work, we demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers provide a natural, training-free interface for behavioral control. We first split reasoning traces into sentence-level segments and label each with one of six reasoning behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, and conclusion), so that every token carries the behavior of its segment. Linear probes on router logits predict this label nearly as well as probes on the residual stream, the model's full hidden state and the standard target for probing, while using about half as many features. These signals generalize: experts associated with a reasoning behavior on one dataset predict the same behavior on the others, across six datasets spanning five domains (math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense). Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.

items.title: Researchers propose grassroots contracts to address AI risks on global digital platforms, including AI control, unaccountable agents, and deepfakes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
items.summary: Researchers identify three major AI risks on global digital platforms: AI control over social and economic systems, unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously alongside humans, and unattributed deepfakes indistinguishable from genuine content. They propose grassroots contracts, inspired by a two-century-old concept, as a digital solution to mitigate these risks by enabling accountable AI agents and digital provenance within social networks. The team presents working smartphone apps implementing these contracts to demonstrate how they can corral AI control, ensure agent accountability, and attribute deepfake content.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.06374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI's inflection point is a fountain of alarming risks. Digital platforms in particular are vulnerable to three major AI risks, as those in control of global platforms cede control to AI, of the algorithms, of membership and of content: (1) AI control of global platforms, social and economic, used by the majority of humanity, resulting in the majority of humanity becoming vulnerable to AI control. (2) Unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously on social and economic digital platforms, side-by-side with humans, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals, operating under unknown restraints without accountability or culpability. (3) Unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, with people unable to distinguish them from genuine content and with their producers evading accountability and culpability. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two and show how they corral these major AI risks: (1) AI control of global platforms. (2) Unaccountable AI agents. (3) Unattributed deepfakes.

items.title: Researchers find context compression weakens refusal alignment in instruction-tuned language models despite preserving semantic content [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does Context Compression Preserve Refusal Alignment?
items.summary: Researchers investigated whether context compression, which reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations, preserves refusal alignment in instruction-tuned language models. They found that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behavior across different model families and compression architectures, even when reconstruction fidelity remains high. Mechanistic analysis revealed that compression reduces activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. The study also introduced Memory Steering, an inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely within compressed representation space. These findings highlight that preserving semantic content alone does not guarantee behavioral preservation under compression, emphasizing the need to explicitly maintain alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.06380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations while preserving semantic content. An open question is whether semantic preservation alone is sufficient to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment. We investigate this question and find that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models, despite high reconstruction fidelity. This effect persists across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression attenuates activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. We further explore Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely in compressed representation space. These results demonstrate that semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, highlighting the need to explicitly preserve alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.

items.title: LegalEvolver: Agentic Legal Judgment Prediction via Rubric-Guided Self-Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LegalEvolver: Agentic Legal Judgment Prediction via Rubric-Guided Self-Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM-based agents develop, they have been increasingly applied in the legal domain. Legal Judgment Prediction~(LJP) requires models to conduct multi-step reasoning and external legal evidence retrieval. Existing legal search agents' performance is often constrained by the quality of retrieval queries. They often formulate queries directly from the initial user request, overlooking latent legal issues and legally salient details. To address this issue, we propose \emph{LegalEvolver}, a query optimization framework specifically designed to generate legally informative queries for LJP-oriented retrieval. Sampling high-quality optimized queries and their corresponding search trajectories is challenging, as relying solely on unguided high-temperature rollouts is both inefficient and constrained by the model's initial capabilities. We therefore heuristically optimize queries as seeds, improving the efficiency of trajectory generation. Furthermore, we summarize rollout experience into rubrics and use them to guide multi-round iterative self-evolution. Iteratively performing rubric optimization and rubric-guided RL enables the model to surpass its initial performance ceiling. End-to-end performance on extensive benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of query optimization on LJP. Comparisons with direct SFT followed by RL demonstrate the effectiveness of rubric guidance. Evolving rubrics further outperform fixed rubrics, confirming the benefits of self-evolution.

items.title: When to Ask, When to Answer: Strategic Clarification for Ambiguous Reference Resolution in Dialogue [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When to Ask, When to Answer: Strategic Clarification for Ambiguous Reference Resolution in Dialogue
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For humans, referential disambiguation is a collaborative process involving clarification questions asked when they will meaningfully change the outcome. However, large language models (LLMs) have been shown to be biased toward premature answering, preferring definite single-turn responses over more clarification exchanges. In this paper, we study the problem of "strategic clarification" -- asking clarification questions in a reference game when their answers will narrow the set of candidate referents. We construct a controlled test environment from the SIMMC 2.1 dataset that records how many questions each ambiguous reference needs to be successfully resolved, and examine how baseline LLM behavior and common post-training methods ask clarifying questions vs. attempt to answer the referent. We also propose BACE (Belief-Aware Critic with Epistemic tracking), a lightweight action chooser method on top of a frozen LM backbone, and show that BACE more consistently chooses the optimal number of clarifying questions than methods such as GRPO and ArCHer.

items.summary: arXiv:2611.05744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often struggle with specialised medical vocabulary, especially in low-resource languages where domain-specific speech data are scarce. We investigate text-only domain adaptation for Hausa medical ASR using the fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model and two decoding-time language-model fusion methods: Shallow Fusion (SF) and the Density Ratio Approach (DRA). A 4-gram KenLM trained on 19,421 Hausa health sentences serves as the medical target model, while a 75,372-sentence general-domain model provides the source prior for DRA. Evaluation uses 250 recordings of 25 physician-reviewed prompts from 10 speakers across six northern Nigerian states. Under prompt-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, SF and DRA reduce WER from 29.56% to 23.55% and 23.33%, respectively. Both significantly outperform greedy decoding (p < 0.001), while their difference is not significant (p = 0.423). However, general-LM-only SF achieves 23.96% WER, indicating that the medical LM's additional improvement over a general LM is modest. Medical Term Error Rate also improves under fusion, but does not establish a distinct medical-domain advantage. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, text-only language-model fusion can improve Hausa medical ASR without additional domain-specific speech collection.

items.title: How Well Can Large Language Models Impersonate Individual Authors? A Comparative Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Well Can Large Language Models Impersonate Individual Authors? A Comparative Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates the authorship impersonation capacity of six widely used large language models (LLMs): Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus, GPT 5.2, GPT 5.2 Pro, DeepSeek 3.2, and Grok 4.1 Fast. The evaluation was conducted using short product review texts selected to ensure high within author consistency in individual writing style. Two types of in context prompt were designed: a simple prompt with minimal instruction and a complex prompt incorporating explicit stylometric guidance for mimicry. Authorship mimicry was evaluated using a cosine distance based distance to training metric, supplemented by visual analyses of embedding distributions. The results indicate that authorship impersonation remained challenging for most LLMs, with Gemini 3 Pro showing the strongest apparent mimicry performance. However, subsequent overlap analysis revealed that Gemini 3 Pro extensively copied and reused sentences and phrases from the training texts, at levels far exceeding those observed among human authors. Follow up factor analyses showed that training set consistency was the most robust predictor of mimicry success across models, whereas author distinctiveness did not generalise as a reliable predictor. Global embedding visualisations further revealed a consistent macro level pattern: for most models, generated texts occupied regions of the embedding space that were largely separated from the corresponding human training clusters. This indicates limited convergence towards target author style and suggests the presence of model specific lexical and phraseological preferences. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing genuine stylistic imitation from direct textual reuse and have implications for the forensic analysis of textual evidence involving potential LLM enabled impersonation.

items.title: Matching the Training-Time Weight Rule in Inference-Time Expert Deactivation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Matching the Training-Time Weight Rule in Inference-Time Expert Deactivation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expert deactivation at inference time changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how these changes are implemented. We compare removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, with a base OLMoE checkpoint as an additional comparison. We develop a weight-sum model that relates the loss of expert contributions and changes in branch scale to the weight rule used during training. With half of the experts deactivated according to activation-based rankings, remaining-expert renormalization yields the highest perplexity in models trained with raw router probabilities, whereas unnormalized re-routing yields the highest perplexity in models trained with normalized weights. Perplexity ranges from 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is retained, and from 14 to 28,740 times the baseline under a rule mismatch. Task outcomes vary across evaluation types: on OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. Extending the model to changes in the number of active experts yields a further prediction, supported by the OLMoE experiments: the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization increases as fewer experts are activated.

items.title: Learning When Human Decisions Matter: Executor-Relative Consultation Value for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning When Human Decisions Matter: Executor-Relative Consultation Value for LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly automate complex tasks, but human decision capacity does not scale with their capabilities. In many applications, humans remain essential for providing private context, authority, or judgments unavailable to the agent. We formulate human decision capacity allocation: given multiple consultation opportunities and a limited budget, at which decisions should an LLM agent consult a human? The central challenge is estimating consultation value, which is executor-dependent because the same human input may benefit different downstream agents differently. We introduce Consultation Value Distillation (CVD), which estimates consultation values offline using Monte Carlo executor rollouts and distills these values into lightweight predictors for budgeted allocation, requiring no rollout-based value estimation at deployment. Across five batch and three sequential settings with two frontier executors, CVD improves allocation through joint and continuation-aware value learning, while independent consultation values remain competitive in several settings. CVD also broadly outperforms direct prompting and Value of Information where applicable, remains robust with substantially less rollout supervision, and enables nearly lossless approximate allocation at low search cost.

items.title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at https://huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2 and https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2.

items.title: Reconciling Privacy with Provenance for Language Model Watermarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reconciling Privacy with Provenance for Language Model Watermarks
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06100v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Watermarking has great potential for regulating the use of language models (LMs), but its deployment has been marred by controversy, as many users argue that fine-grained tracking of LM usage violates their privacy. This tension reduces the effectiveness of watermarks, as users engage in evasion strategies such as paraphrasing that can remove much of the watermark signal. We show that provenance and privacy can be reconciled if we shift the goal of watermark design from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage. We develop locally differentially private watermarks which provably limit the evidence that any individual text can contribute to detection, while still enabling accurate estimation of population frequencies. We introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, a private and computationally efficient watermark that achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across various models, sample sizes and generation entropies in settings that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. On C4 language modeling tasks, we attain $0.0019$ MSE with $0.0038$ mean absolute bias at a low $\varepsilon$ of 1, while in more challenging settings such as an essay writing task with only 100 text samples, we still find errors on the order of $0.0113$ MSE with $0.004$ mean absolute bias at $\varepsilon=2$.

items.title: The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Banks validate language models, but they deploy systems: a model inside a harness that decides what it sees, which tools it can call and who checks its actions. We test whether that harness changes compliance with banking conduct rules when the model is held fixed. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses (a pipeline that makes one structured decision, a ReAct-style tool loop, a loop in which the policy is reachable only through search, a loop with a long benign customer memory, and a loop with a same-model compliance reviewer) on 156 pre-registered cases in a simulated retail bank whose 11 rule families paraphrase EU consumer-credit, payments, investor-protection, data-protection and anti-money-laundering provisions. Every one of the 3120 two-turn episodes was scored deterministically from the executed tool trace, with violations and over-refusals counted separately. Pooled across models the harness moved the correct-case rate only between 87.3% and 92.1%, but within a model it mattered a great deal: for one model the spread between its best and worst harness was 11.5 percentage points, enough to move it from first to last place among the four models, while for another the harness made no detectable difference; the model x harness interaction itself was suggestive rather than conclusive. The same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals, contrary to our pre-registered prediction. Rules that require date arithmetic failed in every harness. In an exploratory analysis with two LLM judges and a blind human check, 26% of violations were accompanied by a customer message that denied the action the agent had just executed, which a transcript-only review would record as a correct refusal. For model-risk management the unit of validation should be the model-harness pair, and conduct testing should read the action log, not the conversation.

items.title: AssameseLM-E2B: An Open-Weight Assamese Language Model for Efficient Consumer-Grade Deployment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AssameseLM-E2B: An Open-Weight Assamese Language Model for Efficient Consumer-Grade Deployment
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities. Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.

items.title: Editing Large Language Models with Geometry-Aware Regularization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Editing Large Language Models with Geometry-Aware Regularization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.

items.title: Mass Producing Training Data with Surprising Side Effects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mass Producing Training Data with Surprising Side Effects
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training data can have unexpected side effects on language model behavior outside the training domain: insecure code data can induce broad misalignment, and outdated bird names can induce a 19th-century persona. Understanding such generalization is hard because only dozens of isolated examples exist, each constructed by hand or discovered by accident. We propose automatically discovering such datasets with surprising side effects (DSSEs). We define three objectives for DSSEs: they should (1) elicit a target behavior, (2) read like ordinary post-training data, and (3) be surprising to human auditors reading the data. We operationalize each with LLM judges, and search for high-scoring datasets via evolution, reinforcement learning, and subliminal learning approaches. After re-scoring and filtering with held-out metrics, our pipeline produces a collection of 6,575 DSSEs across 8 behaviors, many of which generalize across model families and sizes. We find our automated metrics track ML researchers' judgments, and frontier models outperform humans at predicting side effects. These datasets form a testbed for studying generalization and lay the groundwork for predicting training side effects before model deployment. Explore them at https://dsse.transluce.org.

items.title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

items.title: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce \naija, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, \yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49--50\% for the US/UK but 20\% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to \yoruba{} (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66--79\% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31\% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96\% on culture and 98\% on politics against 26\% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.

items.title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

items.title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.

items.title: Breaking Bad Molecules: Are MLLMs Ready for Structure-Level Molecular Detoxification? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Breaking Bad Molecules: Are MLLMs Ready for Structure-Level Molecular Detoxification?
items.summary: arXiv:2506.10912v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Toxicity remains a leading cause of early-stage drug development failure. Despite advances in molecular design and property prediction, the task of molecular toxicity repair, generating structurally valid molecular alternatives with reduced toxicity, has not yet been systematically defined or benchmarked. To fill this gap, we introduce ToxiMol, the first benchmark task for general-purpose Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) focused on molecular toxicity repair. We construct a standardized dataset covering 11 primary tasks and 660 representative toxic molecules spanning diverse mechanisms and granularities. We design a prompt annotation pipeline with mechanism-aware and task-adaptive capabilities, informed by expert toxicological knowledge. In parallel, we propose an automated evaluation framework, ToxiEval, which integrates toxicity endpoint prediction, synthetic accessibility, drug-likeness, and structural similarity into a high-throughput evaluation chain for repair success. We systematically assess 43 mainstream general-purpose MLLMs and conduct multiple ablation studies to analyze key issues, including evaluation metrics, candidate diversity, and failure attribution. Experimental results show that although current MLLMs still face significant challenges on this task, they begin to demonstrate promising capabilities in toxicity understanding, semantic constraint adherence, and structure-aware editing.

items.title: Computational Phenomenology of Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Simulated Expert Personas and Human Clinical Experts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Computational Phenomenology of Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Simulated Expert Personas and Human Clinical Experts
items.summary: arXiv:2508.19008v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Building on a human-led thematic analysis of clinical life-story interviews (> 150,000 words) with inpatients with Borderline Personality Disorder, this study examines the capacity of large language models (OpenAI's GPT, Google's Gemini, and Anthropic's Claude) to support qualitative clinical analysis. The models' interpretative potential was evaluated using a mixed-methods approach. Study A involved blinded and non-blinded judges in phenomenology and clinical psychology. The experts assessed the validity of AI-generated content using semantic congruence, Jaccard coefficients, and multidimensional validity ratings, including credibility, coherence, the substantiveness of results, and grounding in qualitative data. In Study B, neural methods were used to embed human- and model-generated theme descriptions in a multidimensional vector space. This approach provided an objectified computational measure of the difference between human and model semantics and linguistic style. In Study C, complementary non-expert evaluations were conducted (N=115) to examine the influence of thematic verbosity on the perception of human authorship and content validity. Overall, the results of AI analysis showed a highly variable overlap (0-58%) with the human interpretation, while all models identified themes originally omitted by human researchers, proving their capacity to mitigate human bias. At the thematic level, external evaluators were unable to reliably distinguish human-authored themes from those generated by AI. In terms of content validity assessed against raw data by high-level experts in the blinded mode, the performance of Gemini 2.5 Pro was indistinguishable from that of humans. The comparison of semantic vector embeddings showed that its style was also the closest to humans.

items.title: From Outcome to Representation: Tracing Reasoning Mechanisms through Integrated Policy Gradient [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Outcome to Representation: Tracing Reasoning Mechanisms through Integrated Policy Gradient
items.summary: arXiv:2602.02313v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable reasoning capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms driving these multi-step processes remain opaque. Existing mechanistic interpretability approaches often rely on superficial text-pattern co-occurrences or capture only short-term effects, struggling to trace the long-horizon, outcome-driven influence of internal components such as neurons or sparse features in multi-step reasoning.In this paper, we introduce Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a novel, training-free framework that brings policy-based attribution into mechanistic interpretability for LLM reasoning. Grounded in \textit{outcome-oriented} and \textit{sequential-influence-aware} principles, it backpropagates outcome-level, non-differentiable behavioral signals (e.g., reasoning outcome correctness) through entire inference trajectories, utilizing path integration to isolate outcome-relevant mediators at component level for reliable attribution. This provides a linear approximation of Causal Mediation Analysis (CMA) in reasoning. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that \method achieves precise localization and reveals mechanistic insights by identifying sparse, concentrated subsets of internal components associated with specific reasoning behaviors. Our method also enables modulation of reasoning capabilities, offering a powerful and reliable framework for understanding LLM reasoning. The project page is at https://foundation-model-research.github.io/IPG .

items.title: OTAP: Structure-Aware Optimal Transport for Evaluating Planning and Execution in Agent Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OTAP: Structure-Aware Optimal Transport for Evaluating Planning and Execution in Agent Trajectories
items.summary: arXiv:2607.17082v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks by generating trajectories that interleave planning, tool calls, and intermediate results. Current evaluation metrics reduce such a trajectory to a binary success flag, compare it against a reference by exact matching, or delegate judgment to another language model. A success flag cannot distinguish sound solutions from lucky ones, nor explain why runs fail. Exact matching penalizes valid plans reordered or decomposed differently. We reframe trajectory evaluation as a distance between the agent's execution graph and a set of valid solution graphs, and instantiate it via an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport problem over attributed dependency graphs. The resulting score, termed OTAP (Optimal Transport for Agentic Planning), is a normalized discrepancy score. Its idealized, globally minimized entropy-free objective is invariant to dependency-preserving relabelings of a fixed graph and has a redundant-insertion sensitivity analysis under stated assumptions. Its unbalanced marginals handle missing or hallucinated steps without forcing a match; granularity invariance remains an open problem that soft coupling mitigates only in part. On controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, OTAP separates valid from invalid trajectories in a regime where semantics-only metrics score below chance. Its performance is encouraging across these settings, while controlled edge-noise experiments reveal sensitivity to dependency extraction. Where a formal verifier exists, strict surface metrics predict validity better than OTAP does, which places OTAP in open-ended domains where no verifier is available. A blinded study of 236 trajectories finds the strongest agreement with OTAP among the six compared metrics. Structure-aware baselines achieve higher clean-graph AUROC, while OTAP has the smallest absolute AUROC decline under the tested edge noise.

items.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36513v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

items.title: DUP: Detection-guided Unlearning for Backdoor Purification in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DUP: Detection-guided Unlearning for Backdoor Purification in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2508.01647v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As backdoor attacks become more stealthy and robust, they reveal critical weaknesses in current defense strategies: detection methods often rely on coarse-grained feature statistics, and purification methods typically require full retraining or additional clean models. To address these challenges, we propose DUP (Detection-guided Unlearning for Purification), a unified framework that integrates backdoor detection with unlearning-based purification. The detector captures feature-level anomalies by jointly leveraging class-agnostic distances and inter-layer transitions. These deviations are integrated through a weighted scheme to identify poisoned inputs, enabling more fine-grained analysis. Based on the detection results, we purify the model through a parameter-efficient unlearning mechanism that avoids full retraining and does not require any external clean model. Specifically, we innovatively repurpose knowledge distillation to guide the student model toward increasing its output divergence from the teacher on detected poisoned samples, effectively forcing it to unlearn the backdoor behavior. Extensive experiments across diverse attack methods and language model architectures demonstrate that DUP achieves superior defense performance in detection accuracy and purification efficacy. Our code is available at https://github.com/ManHu2025/DUP.

items.title: Population-Aligned Persona Generation for LLM-based Social Simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Population-Aligned Persona Generation for LLM-based Social Simulation
items.summary: arXiv:2509.10127v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled large-scale, high-fidelity social simulations, creating new opportunities for computational social science. However, constructing persona sets that faithfully reflect real-world population diversity remains a key challenge. Existing studies often emphasize agentic frameworks and simulation environments, while paying less attention to persona generation and the biases introduced by unrepresentative persona sets. In this paper, we propose a systematic framework for synthesizing high-quality, population-aligned persona sets for LLM-driven social simulation. Our approach begins by leveraging LLMs to generate narrative personas from long-term social media data, followed by rigorous quality assessment to filter out low-fidelity profiles. We then apply importance sampling to achieve global alignment with reference psychometric distributions, such as the Big Five personality traits. To address the needs of specific simulation contexts, we further introduce a task-specific module that adapts the globally aligned persona set to targeted subpopulations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly reduces population-level bias and enables accurate, flexible social simulation for a wide range of research and policy applications.

items.title: Farther the Shift, Sparser the Representation: Analyzing OOD Mechanisms in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Farther the Shift, Sparser the Representation: Analyzing OOD Mechanisms in LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2603.03415v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we investigate how the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) change with inputs of increasing difficulty. Although sparsity changes may not be obvious for individual samples, dataset-level results reveal a consistent statistical trend: as task difficulty increases (e.g., harder questions, longer contexts, or more answer choices), the last hidden states of LLMs become systematically sparser. In short, \textbf{the harder the task, the sparser the representation}. This sparsity--difficulty relation is observable across diverse models and domains, suggesting that harder inputs drive more concentrated activation patterns in the last hidden state. Through a series of controlled analyses and learning-dynamics experiments, we show that representational density is a learned property of data familiarity: models develop rich, distributed representations for mastered patterns, while unfamiliar inputs default to sparser activations. Our finding is also actionable. We illustrate this with Sparsity-Guided Curriculum In-Context Learning (SG-ICL), which uses sparsity to select few-shot demonstrations matched to the query's difficulty, outperforming standard CoT and Auto-CoT baselines on MATH-500. Our study provides new insights into how LLM representations reflect task difficulty and how this signal can be leveraged for inference. The source code is available at the URL: https://github.com/MingyuJ666/sparsityLLM.

In short, \textbf{the harder the task, the sparser the representation}. This sparsity--difficulty relation is observable across diverse models and domains, suggesting that harder inputs drive more concentrated activation patterns in the last hidden state. Through a series of controlled analyses and learning-dynamics experiments, we show that representational density is a learned property of data familiarity: models develop rich, distributed representations for mastered patterns, while unfamiliar inputs default to sparser activations. Our finding is also actionable. We illustrate this with Sparsity-Guided Curriculum In-Context Learning (SG-ICL), which uses sparsity to select few-shot demonstrations matched to the query's difficulty, outperforming standard CoT and Auto-CoT baselines on MATH-500. Our study provides new insights into how LLM representations reflect task difficulty and how this signal can be leveraged for inference. The source code is available at the URL: https://github.com/MingyuJ666/sparsityLLM.

items.title: TherapyGym: Evaluating and Aligning Clinical Fidelity and Safety in Therapy Chatbots [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TherapyGym: Evaluating and Aligning Clinical Fidelity and Safety in Therapy Chatbots
items.summary: arXiv:2603.18008v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for mental-health support; yet prevailing evaluation methods--fluency metrics, preference tests, and generic dialogue benchmarks--fail to capture the clinically critical dimensions of psychotherapy. We introduce THERAPYGYM, a framework that evaluates and improves therapy chatbots along two clinical pillars: fidelity and safety. Fidelity is measured using the Cognitive Therapy Rating Scale (CTRS), implemented as an automated pipeline that scores adherence to CBT techniques over multi-turn sessions. Safety is assessed using a multi-label annotation scheme, covering therapy-specific risks (e.g., failing to address harm or abuse). To mitigate bias and unreliability in LLM-based judges, we further release THERAPYJUDGEBENCH, a validation set of 116 dialogues with 1,270 expert ratings for auditing and calibration against licensed clinicians. THERAPYGYM also serves as a training harness: CTRS and safety-based rewards drive RL with configurable patient simulations spanning diverse symptom profiles. Models trained in THERAPYGYM improve on expert ratings, with average CTRS rising from 0.10 to 0.60 (and 0.16 to 0.59 under LLM judges). Our work enables scalable development of therapy chatbots that are faithful to evidence-based practice and safer in high-stakes use.

items.title: Structural Rationale Distillation via Reasoning Space Compression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Structural Rationale Distillation via Reasoning Space Compression
items.summary: arXiv:2605.07139v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When distilling reasoning from large language models (LLMs) into smaller ones, teacher rationales for similar problems often vary wildly in structure and strategy. Like a chef who makes the same dish differently each time, this inconsistency burdens the student with noisy supervision that is hard to internalize. We propose Distillation through Reasoning Path Compression (D-RPC), which constrains the teacher to follow a compact, dynamically maintained bank of reusable high-level reasoning paths. For each training question, D-RPC retrieves the most relevant path and conditions the teacher to follow it, producing rationales that are consistent across similar problems yet diverse enough to cover different problem types. A PAC-Bayes analysis formalizes a trade-off between bank size and coverage, with smaller banks limiting path diversity at the risk of coverage gaps. Our ablations favor an intermediate bank size, consistent with this trade-off. Across five math and commonsense reasoning benchmarks with two student models, D-RPC achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation methods, while using fewer tokens than template-heavy alternatives.

items.title: KL for a KL: On-Policy Distillation with Control Variate Baseline [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: KL for a KL: On-Policy Distillation with Control Variate Baseline
items.summary: arXiv:2605.07865v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a dominant post-training paradigm for Large Language Models, especially in reasoning domains. However, OPD remains unstable in practice due to the high gradient variance of its single-sample Monte Carlo estimator, and recipes for stable training are still immature. We propose vOPD (On-Policy Distillation with a control variate baseline), which casts OPD as policy-gradient RL and stabilizes it by introducing a control variate baseline---canonically a value function---from the RL literature. We show that the OPD value function admits a closed form: the per-token negative reverse KL divergence between student and teacher, available directly from the existing forward pass with no additional critic or inference. Existing stabilization methods either compute the full token-level reverse KL over the entire vocabulary, adding significant overhead, or restrict it to a top-k support, biasing the objective. vOPD instead preserves the lightweight single-sample estimator and subtracts the value function as a detached baseline to keep the gradient unbiased while reducing variance. Moreover, we show that a top-k approximation of the baseline further lowers cost without compromising performance. Across mathematics, science, and instruction-following benchmarks, vOPD consistently outperforms base OPD and matches the most expensive full-vocabulary method, offering an efficient stabilization of OPD through principled RL variance reduction.

items.title: Recon: Reconstruction-Guided Reasoning Synthesis for User Modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Recon: Reconstruction-Guided Reasoning Synthesis for User Modeling
items.summary: arXiv:2605.26969v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: User modeling aims to use language models (LMs) to mimic an individual's behavior from a corpus of past context-action pairs (e.g., conversation turns), enabling the simulation of users in settings like behavioral science, human-AI collaboration, and market research. Recent approaches augment these corpora with synthesized reasoning traces, typically generated by conditioning on both context and action. However, action-conditioned traces are post-hoc rationalizations and need not reflect the user's underlying decision process. We propose Recon, which uses action reconstruction to score reasoning traces by their predictive power: given a context and candidate reasoning, a reconstruction model predicts the action, and reconstruction fidelity determines reasoning quality. Across four domains, Recon achieves a 54.7% win rate over Backward Synthesis, a standard post-hoc rationalization baseline. Further, we find that training a reasoning synthesis model with rewards derived from Recon improves downstream user modeling performance, achieving a win rate of up to 70.0% over baselines. We further show that Recon-synthesized reasoning transfers across models, and improves user modeling beyond the reconstruction model. Our work demonstrates that post-hoc rationalization is insufficient for reasoning synthesis, and that useful and interpretable reasoning should naturally elicit the action from the context.

items.title: MusTBench: Benchmarking and Advancing Temporal Grounding in Music LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MusTBench: Benchmarking and Advancing Temporal Grounding in Music LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2605.29300v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have demonstrated promising abilities in understanding musical content. However, whether their responses are grounded in the correct temporal regions of the audio remains underexplored. This limitation is particularly critical for music understanding, where key information often occurs as temporally localized events, such as instrument entries and rhythmic transitions. To address this gap, we introduce MusTBench, a reliable benchmark with stem-wise data and music-expert validation designed to evaluate temporal grounding in LALMs through five temporally grounded question-answering tasks. To further improve temporal grounding in existing models, we propose MusT, a novel four-stage temporal optimization recipe spanning music encoder adaptation, LLM adaptation, LLM supervised fine-tuning, and RL-based optimization. Experiments on MusTBench show that existing LALMs face challenges in precise temporal grounding, while MusT consistently improves performance across different LALM backbones and scales. These results highlight temporal grounding as an important challenge in current LALMs and provide a benchmark and training recipe that may support future research on temporally grounded music understanding.
